title: Drought, Prayer, and a Hard No
overview: During a severe drought, Jeremiah and his people plead with God for help, but God refuses, condemns prophets who promise easy peace, and warns that worse disaster is coming.

parts.label: A land without rain (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Servants find the cisterns empty (pits dug to catch rainwater), farmers cannot work the cracked ground, and people cover their heads, a sign of grief and shame. Even wild animals suffer, as the doe, known for caring for her young, abandons her newborn because there is no grass.

parts.label: A plea despite guilt (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The speaker admits the people have done wrong and asks God to act for his own name, meaning for his honor and reputation rather than because they deserve it. They ask why God seems like a passing traveler who does not care, or a warrior caught off guard and unable to help.

parts.label: God refuses to listen (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: God answers that the people love to wander, which most readers take as chasing other gods, and tells Jeremiah not even to pray for them. Fasting and temple offerings will not change things, because war, famine and disease are coming.

parts.label: Prophets who promise peace (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Jeremiah objects that other prophets keep telling the people all will be well, as if to say the people are being misled. God says those prophets are making it up, and that they and their listeners will die and be left unburied, which was seen as a terrible disgrace.

parts.label: Tears for a wounded people (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Jeremiah is to weep without stopping for his nation, pictured as a young daughter badly wounded, as he imagines war dead in the fields and starving people in the city. The last line is unclear in Hebrew: it may mean prophets and priests will be taken into exile, or that they wander about without understanding.

parts.label: One more plea (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The people ask whether God has rejected them for good, confess their own and their ancestors' wrongs, and appeal to God's covenant (the binding agreement between God and Israel) and to his throne, probably meaning Jerusalem or its temple. They end by saying that idols cannot bring rain and the sky cannot do it on its own, so their only hope is the LORD.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the people's confessions here are genuine repentance that God still turns down, or words that did not match their lives, and that choice shapes how they understand God's refusal to hear them.
think: When someone says sorry only after things have gone badly for them, how do you tell whether they really mean it?
